slides.title: Tech and Sun: the first commitment cycle

items.text: What commitment pooling is, how Green Goods implements it, and how G$ moves through Tech and Sun.

notes: The deck moves from commitment pooling as Grassroots Economics describes it, to how Green Goods implements it, to the money and how it circulates through Tech and Sun.
It ends with a pause to decide the shape of the Tech and Sun pool and the workshop that writes the first commitments.
Source: review of 2026-09-03.

slides.title: Six things a pool does
slides.lead: Grassroots Economics names six functions. In plain words:

items.sub: Choosing what the pool recognises: which people, promises and things count.
Saying how promises compare, so a workshop and a solar check can be weighed.
Matching promises to real capacity, so no one promises more than they can keep.
Letting promises be offered, taken up, passed on and settled.
Closing a promise with a receipt anyone can check.
When a promise slips, changing or repaying it in the open.

notes: In Grassroots Economics' own wording, curation identifies which commitments, people, businesses, vouchers and assets the community is prepared to recognise; valuation expresses how a pool recognises the relative value of different commitments; limitation connects trust with actual capacity; exchange allows commitments to be seeded, swapped, routed, fulfilled and settled.
Fulfillment closes an obligation and leaves an auditable receipt, and delays and changes can enter transparent processes of repair.
Green Goods uses the same six names.
Source: Grassroots Economics, Circling Back (2026-08-12); Ruddick, Proto-Social Infrastructure and Stewardship of Commitment Pooling (IJCCR, 2026).

slides.title: One village pool: Binguni, Kenya
slides.lead: About 400 households pooled seeds, water, cooking and labour, worth over 50,000 KES a month.

items.sub: Every pledge was counted, like 10 kg of seeds worth 2,500 KES.
A cap of 50,000 vouchers, 2,300 per member, 4,000 held in reserve.
Women farmers in nearby Mbele accepted the vouchers for labour.
2 percent monthly decay, so vouchers circulate rather than sit.

notes: The community decided what went into the pool, how each pledge was counted, and the caps; that is curation, valuation and limitation in one village.
Green Goods records promises and supports them with G$ instead of issuing vouchers, so the lesson is the shape of the pool, not the token.
Source: Grassroots Economics case study, Commitment Pooling in Binguni and Mbele, docs.grassecon.org (2026-06-04).

slides.title: In Green Goods, a promise is an Offer or a Request
slides.lead: Someone offers, someone asks, and someone else confirms it was kept. The pool remembers who promised what, and who kept it.

items.sub: I will run a weekly climate discussion.
Someone keep the monthly solar log.
Another person confirms it; the record stays.

columns.text: It is not a currency. Money, like G$, can support a kept promise, but the promise comes first.

notes: This is how Green Goods implements the pool: an Offer and a Request are the two directions of one promise, and a promise is kept when someone other than the promiser confirms it.
Grassroots Economics traces the pattern to rotational labour groups in Kenya, where neighbours pool promises of work and keep track of who has been helped.
Source: Ruddick, Commitment Pooling: an economic protocol inspired by ancestral wisdom (IJCCR, 2023); plan hub contract-spec.md registers #19 and #20.

slides.title: A pool belongs to a garden and runs in cycles
slides.lead: Tech and Sun is a garden; its gardeners are the members. The Tech and Sun pool is theirs.

items.sub: The pool's long run, usually a quarter. One open at a time.
A shorter run for one purpose, like a course cohort. Several can run alongside.
Made inside a season or a campaign, or on its own.
Sits above them all; commitments in any cycle answer it.

notes: A pool has at most one open Season and any number of open Campaigns; each cycle ends and the next one is seeded fresh.
A Need can outlast a season, and a commitment points at the Need it answers, so the Need stays attached to the work.
Green Goods also runs a pool of its own, the Green Goods pool, which appears later in the deck.
Source: plan hub uiux-spec.md section 4.2; contract-spec.md section 5.2; community-interface spec.

slides.title: One promise, around the loop

items.sub: the problem and the outcome
the starting point
an Offer or a Request
evidence, then approval
someone else says it was kept
sent on the kept promise
what changed, what people say
the record at the cycle's close

notes: The loop runs from a Need through the baseline, the commitment and the work; any G$ support declared for a promise is sent once someone else confirms the promise was kept.
The certificate comes later, when the cycle closes and the delta and testimony are recorded, so it is the record of the outcome rather than the trigger for support.

Four kinds of promise share this loop: work with evidence, help for someone where the person helped confirms, a season or campaign promise seeded by the steward, and a promise recorded on a gardener's behalf.
The one rule that never changes: nobody confirms their own promise.
Source: plan hub diagrams.md D5; settlement-spec.md section 3.1.3; review of 2026-09-03.

slides.title: Who does what

items.sub: Make promises, do the work, confirm help received.
Names Needs, seeds commitments, runs the pool.
Records the baseline and what changed.
Reads the record. GoodDollar is the first.
Confirms help received, gives testimony.

notes: Gardeners are the members of the garden; the steward runs the pool; the evaluator records the baseline and the delta; funders read the record; the community confirms help and gives testimony.
Nobody confirms their own promise, on any path.
Source: plan hub diagrams.md D4; external-brief-roles in visual-assets.md.

columns.heading: GoodDollar wants
items: More people using G$, and staying

notes: The Good Labs Foundation funds the pilot directly after the DAO vote, GIP-26, did not pass; Green Goods is one of four members with Gardens, ReFi DAO and Textile, and GoodDollar confirmed on August 8 that it wants to see circulation.

slides.title: The Tech and Sun pool: four questions
slides.lead: A pause to decide. Draft answers from the July survey sit under each.

items.sub: Start with the survey drafts. Add only what a gardener will confirm.
Flat for now. G$ support declared per commitment, or none.
Small caps per gardener and per commitment, raised as promises are kept.
The person helped confirms; the steward confirms hub Requests. Support follows the kept promise.

notes: This slide is the pause: the four questions are the decisions the Tech and Sun pool owns, and the drafts under them come from the July survey.
The survey also answered the slipping promise question: repay a different way first, repay later second, talk it through third, forgive fourth, decided case by case with no fixed limit.
G$ support declared for a promise is sent once the promise is confirmed kept; the certificate is the cycle's record and comes later.
Source: July 21 survey; plan hub contract-spec.md amendment 2026-08-01; settlement-spec.md section 3.1.3.
